**1\. Introduction** 

**1.1 Laboratory Overview** 

In this lab, we will remake the audio player with the following features: 

• Users will be able play 8 different songs using four buttons 

• Users will be able to stop and replay the song from the audio player 

• Users will be able to display the name of a song that is being played in the LCD • Users will be able to display a confirmation message when choosing the song in the LCD • Users will have 5 seconds to confirm the song that they want to play 

• Users will be able to see the state of the audio player using RGB LEDs (playing song, waiting for next  song, no playing song) 

• Users will display the instructions for using the audio player via UART 

• Users will be able to adjust the volume of a song  

• Users will be able to execute these features in three threads 

By the end of this project you will have built your own “MP3 player” and you should feel confident about  the techniques and concepts that you have learned during this course. 

**2\. Requirements** 

In this lab, we will be using the following hardware, software, and firmware:  

• **PlatformIO** 

• **STM32 Framework. Arduino Framework is Prohibited.** 

• **FreeRTOS or Zephyr OS** 

• **RT-Thread RT-Spark Development Board** 

• A breadboard, 4 x 330 Ω resistors, 4 x buttons, 1 x 100Ω resistor, 1 x 10kΩ potentiometer,1 x LCD,  1 x speaker (ABI-001-RC).

**3\. Hardware Setup** 

**3.1 Board Layout** 

**![][image1]Figure 1.1 The RT-Thread Development Board Peripherals Layout** 

Figure 1.1 shows the RT-Spark Development Board peripheral layout, including all modules attached to  the board. In this laboratory activity, you will utilize the following peripherals present in the development  board: (i) 240x240 LCD on-board display, (ii) 3.5mm headphone jack to be connected into an external  speaker, (iii) an external potentiometer, 5 external push buttons, (iv) three external LEDs (i.e., RED,  GREEN, and BLUE LEDs), and (v) UART Pins (i.e., RX and TX on-board pins).

Shown in figures 1.2, 1.3, and 1.4 are the configuration of the external potentiometer, external push buttons  using pull-up resistor, and the RGB LEDs setup in either common anode or common cathode setups. 

![][image5]Figure 1.4 RT-Spark LCD Connection Diagram Part 1 

![][image6]  
Figure 1.5 RT-Spark LCD Connection Diagram Part 2 

Shown in figures 1.4 and 1.5 is a 1.3-inch LCD screen of the development board with a resolution of  240x240, providing a very sharp display. The screen uses an ST7789 v3 driver chip, and the communication  interface is an 8080 parallel port. Communication with the microcontroller is achieved through FSMC  simulation of the driver timings. Eight data lines are used for data transmission, and one address select line  serves as the chip's enable signal. 

![][image7]  
Figure 1.6 RT-Spark Audio Codec Module

Prepared by: Paul Rodolf P. Castor, M.Sc. © February 2026   
P a g e | **5** 

Shown in Figure 1.6 is the ES8388 audio code module of the RT-Spark development board, a high performance, low-power stereo audio codec by Everest Semiconductor, featuring 2-channel ADC/DAC,  microphone amplifiers, and a headphone driver. It supports up to 96 kHz sampling rates and 24-bit  resolution, commonly used in ESP32, STM32, and portable audio devices via I2S and I2C. 

**4\. Final Project**   
In this project, you will build our own “MP3 player”, for the sake of this project, students do not need to  generate the songs. Students should download the following files: (i) NHD\_0216HZ.h (**basis only** since you will be using the on-board LCD display of the development board), (ii) NHD\_0216HZ.cpp (**basis only** since you will be using the on-board LCD display of the development board), (iii) song.h, (iv) song\_def.h  and (v) main.cpp (**basis only** since it uses mbed OS, and you will use FreeRTOS or Zypher OS in this  project). These files should be placed in the same directory. 

**4.1 Song\_def.h** 

There are a total of 10 different songs that have been provided for this lab; each of these songs has its own  name (that has been split into two attributes, name1 and name2), notes, beats, tempos or speed, and length.  In order to access these attributes, you can:  

**\<SONG\>.note\[noteIndex\]** or **\*(\<SONG\>.note \+ noteIndex)** 

**Note:** There are no notes in the songs provided, please take care when dealing with them. It might be  useful to review the module 8 lab solution to remember how to play a song. 

**4.2 Timeout vs Ticker** 

The Ticker interface is used to setup a recurring interrupt to repeatedly call a function at a specified rate whereas Timeout setup an interrupt to a call function after a specified delay. For instance, if we have the  following code: 

![][image8]  
After two seconds led1 and led2 will turn off, but after another two more seconds just led1 will turn on  because the tickerFlip function will execute as long as the program continues while the timeoutFlipper  will just executed once, unless is setup again. 

**4.3 Your Application Code** 

In this exercise, you are required to create your own main.cpp using STM32CubeMX, STM32cubeIDE,  and FreeRTOS or Zephyr RTOS, and utilize the provided main.cpp to perform the following requirements

Prepared by: Paul Rodolf P. Castor, M.Sc. © February 2026   
P a g e | **6** 

below: 

• Define inputs and outputs that are missing. 

• Complete the functions update\_lcd\_leds\_thread(), adjust\_volume() and polling\_buttons(). • Use buttons 2 – 4 to insert a song in binary form from the array of songs. For instance, if the all the  buttons are low or they are zero then we would end up playing the first song. 

• While the buttons (2-4) are being pressed, press button 1 to select a song and then release all the  buttons. 

• Press button 1 again to confirm your choice, if you don’t do anything for 5 seconds, everything will  continue normally. 

• Display name of the song on the LCD when playing and a confirmation message when changing  the song. 

• Use the timeout and ticker interface to wait for the 5 seconds of confirmation and play music  respectively. 

• Use USER\_BUTTON to stop/play a song. 

• When a song is played the blue LED should be on  

• When a song is paused the red LED should be on 

• When changing a song the green LED should be on 

• Create 3 threads to: 

1\. Update the LCD and RGB LEDs 

2\. Polling buttons  

3\. Adjust the volume 

• **Note that:** 

o Every thread contains an infinite loop 

o Tasks are scheduled in a cooperative manner, namely, threads can go to waiting state after  each update, to let the next thread be scheduled 

o Since the LCD must be accessed exclusively, we need a mutex to protect its single access. • In the main program:   
o Clear the LCD display 

o Start all threads 

o Send the instruction of how to use the audio player via UART 

o Use sleep mode to reduce power consumption
